title: PostgreSQL’s "random_page_cost" isn’t just about disk latency — and the default is often right when your indexes are
author: Franck Pachot
body_html:
You may have read that PostgreSQL's default random_page_cost of 4.0 was chosen for HDDs, where random reads incur high seek latency while sequential reads amortize that cost across many pages. The usual advice is to lower it on SSDs, where latency is lower, and the gap between random and sequential access narrows.

But that explanation is incomplete. The ratio reflects more than raw storage speed. At every layer—CPU, RAM, and disk—batched and sequential access is faster than random, scattered access.

In addition to that, concerning random_page_cost and seq_page_cost in PostgreSQL:

  • The planner estimates scan cost from the total number of pages to be accessed, without knowing which pages will come from disk, the OS page cache, or PostgreSQL shared buffers. In a well-tuned production system, much of the working set is already cached, so storage latency applies to only a fraction of the pages being costed. Yet random_page_cost and seq_page_cost are still applied uniformly. That means the SSD-versus-HDD difference is probably less important to this estimate than commonly assumed.
  • Scan cost is not only about read latency. It also reflects memory footprint and cache pollution. Random reads fetch full 8 KB pages, even when an index scan needs only one row, and those pages occupy shared buffers, potentially evicting more useful pages. Repeated scattered lookups can create substantial churn in both shared memory and the OS page cache. Sequential scans are more cache-friendly: PostgreSQL uses a buffer ring strategy for large one-time reads, reusing a small set of buffers rather than polluting the entire cache. For sequential scans, this ring is 256 KB, small enough to fit in L2 cache and still support synchronized scans. Random access gets no comparable protection.

So the default 4:1 ratio captures more than seek time on spinning disks. It also reflects the broader system cost of random access: loading whole pages for partial reads, increased eviction pressure, and the loss of cooperative optimizations such as ring buffers and synchronized scans.

Setting random_page_cost close to seq_page_cost tells the planner that random and sequential access are equally cheap in all those respects, including memory impact, which is usually not true except maybe on oversized systems.

The default 4:1 ratio may be somewhat arbitrary, but it has one practical advantage: it has been the standard for most PostgreSQL users for years. Changing it to match what seems optimal for one specific system adds complexity when comparing systems or migrating workloads between them.

There's also a broader point. The usual recommendation is to bring the ratio close to 1 by setting random_page_cost to 1.1. But in a reliable database, the choice between a full table scan and an index scan should not hinge on such a small variation, because data grows and estimates are never exact. If changing random_page_cost from 4 to 1.1 alters your execution plans, you may be better off improving the index design, since neither access path is clearly superior.

The default settings are: 

postgres=# \dconfig *page_cost

List of configuration parameters
    Parameter     | Value
------------------+-------
 random_page_cost | 4
 seq_page_cost    | 1

(2 rows)

I create a simple table with an index: 

drop table if exists demo
;
create table demo (
 id bigserial primary key,
 type int,
 value float default random() 
);
insert into demo (type)
 select generate_series(1,1e6)%2
;
create index on demo ( type );
;
vacuum analyze demo
;

I'll test multiple values for random_page_cost and flush both caches between each execution to better reflect the fact that disk latency matters. For the Linux buffers, I'll sync and echo 3 to /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches, and for PostgreSQL, I'll call pg_buffercache_evict_all() from the pg_buffercache extension: 

create extension if not exists pg_buffercache
;
select pg_buffercache_evict_all() ;
\! sudo sync && echo 3 | sudo tee /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches

I start with the default random_page_cost=4, and the query planner chooses a Bitmap Index Scan: 

postgres=# select pg_buffercache_evict_all() ;

 pg_buffercache_evict_all
--------------------------
 (6856,1,0)

(1 row)

postgres=# \! sudo sync && echo 3 | sudo tee /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches
3

postgres=# set random_page_cost=4 ;

SET

postgres=# explain (analyze, buffers, summary off)
 select * from demo where type=0
;

         QUERY PLAN
----------------------------------------------------------
 Bitmap Heap Scan on demo  (cost=5628.62..18308.62 rows=504800 width=20) (actual time=25.902..647.733 rows=500000.00 loops=1)
   Recheck Cond: (type = 0)
   Heap Blocks: exact=6370
   Buffers: shared read=6793
   ->  Bitmap Index Scan on demo_type_idx  (cost=0.00..5502.43 rows=504800 width=0) (actual time=23.932..23.933 rows=500000.00 loops=1)
         Index Cond: (type = 0)
         Index Searches: 1
         Buffers: shared read=423

(8 rows)

A Bitmap Index Scan improves random reads by reordering them to avoid reading the same page multiple times and by favoring readahead, so it is probably the most stable plan: it reads only the pages that satisfy the index condition, and never more than the total number of pages in the table.

I continue with this idea of random_page_cost=1.1 closer to seq_page_cost, and the query planner chooses an Index Scan: 

postgres=# select pg_buffercache_evict_all() ;

 pg_buffercache_evict_all
--------------------------
 (6863,0,0)

(1 row)

postgres=# \! sudo sync && echo 3 | sudo tee /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches

3

postgres=# set random_page_cost=1.1 ;

SET

postgres=# explain (analyze, buffers, summary off)
 select * from demo where type=0
;

         QUERY PLAN
----------------------------------------------------------
 Index Scan using demo_type_idx on demo  (cost=0.42..15369.72 rows=504800 width=20) (actual time=2.476..837.685 rows=500000.00 loops=1)
   Index Cond: (type = 0)
   Index Searches: 1
   Buffers: shared read=6793

(4 rows)

When latency does not matter, the query planner skips the overhead of a bitmap scan and switches to an index scan, which is a true random read. However, when all reads come from disk after flushing the cache, it is not faster (837 milliseconds instead of 647), even though it performs the same number of read calls (6,793 pages). The default value of random_page_cost=4 accounts not only for disk latency but also for Linux readahead, which accelerates Bitmap Heap Scan, and we have ignored this when lowering it.

Let's try the opposite, a high value of random_page_cost=40 so that the query planner switches to Seq Scan: 

postgres=# select pg_buffercache_evict_all() ;

 pg_buffercache_evict_all
--------------------------
 (6856,1,0)

(1 row)

postgres=# \! sudo sync && echo 3 | sudo tee /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches
3

postgres=# set random_page_cost=40 ;

SET

postgres=# explain (analyze, buffers, summary off)
 select * from demo where type=0
;

                                                                                                                            QUERY PLAN
----------------------------------------------------------
 Seq Scan on demo  (cost=0.00..18870.00 rows=504800 width=20) (actual time=1.032..529.180 rows=500000.00 loops=1)
   Filter: (type = 0)
   Rows Removed by Filter: 500000
   Buffers: shared read=6370

(4 rows)

In this case, the full table scan was faster (529 milliseconds instead of 837) because it reads the same number of pages (6370) but more efficiently.

I flushed the cache to demonstrate on the myth that the disk latency should drive the settings, but if you run the same without flushing the caches, you will see that the Bitmap Scan will be slightly faster: 

postgres=# set random_page_cost=4 ;        -- the default 
SET
postgres=# explain (analyze, buffers, summary off)
 select * from demo where type=0
;

QUERY PLAN
----------------------------------------------------------
 Bitmap Heap Scan on demo  (cost=5628.62..18308.62 rows=504800 width=20) (actual time=12.219..59.027 rows=500000.00 loops=1)
   Recheck Cond: (type = 0)
   Heap Blocks: exact=6370
   Buffers: shared hit=6793
   ->  Bitmap Index Scan on demo_type_idx  (cost=0.00..5502.43 rows=504800 width=0) (actual time=11.496..11.497 rows=500000.00 loops=1)
         Index Cond: (type = 0)
         Index Searches: 1
         Buffers: shared hit=423
(8 rows)

postgres=# set random_page_cost=1.1 ;      -- smaller (1.1)
SET
postgres=# explain (analyze, buffers, summary off)
 select * from demo where type=0
;

QUERY PLAN
----------------------------------------------------------
 Index Scan using demo_type_idx on demo  (cost=0.42..15369.72 rows=504800 width=20) (actual time=0.022..67.209 rows=500000.00 loops=1)
   Index Cond: (type = 0)
   Index Searches: 1
   Buffers: shared hit=6793
(4 rows)

postgres=# set random_page_cost=40 ;      -- larger (10x)
SET
postgres=# explain (analyze, buffers, summary off)
 select * from demo where type=0
;

QUERY PLAN
----------------------------------------------------------
 Seq Scan on demo  (cost=0.00..18870.00 rows=504800 width=20) (actual time=0.014..67.948 rows=500000.00 loops=1)
   Filter: (type = 0)
   Rows Removed by Filter: 500000
   Buffers: shared hit=6370
(4 rows)

While Seq Scan was the best when all reads came from disk, the Bitmap Heap Scan chosen with default settings is faster with cache hits because the reads come from the PostgreSQL shared buffers, whereas the Seq Scan reads go through the smaller ring buffer. They are faster, but use more memory.

In this demonstration, I adopted the premise that random_page_cost depends on disk latency and flushes the cache to reflect that latency. The results show that the usual recommendation to lower random_page_cost is not correct. For the same number of pages, sequential reads are faster than equivalent random reads, even without mechanical seek latency, because batch processing is optimized at every layer. When the working set fits in memory, as expected in OLTP, the default settings provide the best response time.

Rather than tweaking defaults and introducing more instability into execution plans, you should focus on index definitions. What makes an index faster is its ability to read significantly fewer pages than the total number of pages. The choice between index access and a full table scan should be qualitative rather than quantitative: is it an analytical query that occasionally aggregates many rows, or an OLTP query that frequently fetches a small set of rows?

  • If your query needs to read rows from most of the table pages, as is typical for analytic queries, a Seq Scan will be best for response time and shared buffers memory usage. It will be chosen by the default query planner settings.
  • If your query needs only rows from a small number of pages, as is typical for OLTP, an index should identify the fewest pages to read while covering all selective filters and the pagination order. It will be chosen according to the estimated selectivity.
  • If you are somewhere in between, a Bitmap Index Scan helps reduce the cost of random reads to nearly that of a sequential scan, thanks to prefetching. Lowering random_page_cost can prevent the planner from switching to a Seq Scan that would pollute the filesystem buffers with unnecessary pages. Still, the best approach is to fit into one of the two previous categories. For example, partition pruning may limit a Seq Scan to a single partition, making it the best choice, while an Index Only Scan may reduce the number of pages read, making it the better option.

The user's perception of performance also matters: an index scan takes time proportional to the size of the result set, whereas a sequential scan takes time proportional to the size of the table. In OLTP workloads, users expect small result sets to return quickly and accept that larger ones will take longer. In analytical workloads, where results are typically aggregated, response time is driven more by database size than by the size of the final result, and parallel sequential scans are used to reduce response time when the database grows.

In this demo, I used an index with poor selectivity. With a more selective index, the planner would naturally choose an index scan without any parameter tweaks. If lowering random_page_cost improves performance in your tests, it indicates that your indexes are not selective enough. The planner may be right to avoid them, but switching to a full table scan is not the right outcome either. Forcing index usage may provide a short-term gain, but it will not scale as data grows and memory pressure increases. In the long run, a better index design is a more reliable solution than tuning system parameters to compensate for weak indexing. A selective query should never fall back to a full table scan, not because random_page_cost is set artificially low, but because the index design is good.
